Active galactic nuclei, fueled by massive accretion rates, exhibit highly observable properties, with their central engines exhibiting extreme levels of brightness. The rapid precession of their spinning black holes, characterized by very short periods, has the potential to leave a unique signature in the observed light patterns, allowing for the detection of particles with extremely low mass, as small as $10^{-29}$ times the mass of a proton. By analyzing the lack of observed particles from a specific group of heavy, spinning black holes, as small as 10 to a thousand times the mass of the sun, scientists can begin to map the behavior of these elusive particles, with more accurate parameters becoming available as small as $10^{-31}$ to $10^{-27}$ times the Compton wavelength of a proton.

A difference in retinal thickness between its upper and lower halves is a sign of interkinetic nuclear migration (INM) by retinal progenitor cells. 
These cells show a migratory pattern that corresponds to the distribution of neurogenic factors in the tissue, which INM helps to maximize. 
Recent time-lapse analyses, however, indicate that the Zebrafish INM process may not align with the described migratory behavior of their progenitor cells. 
By applying non-invasive, large-scale time-lapse analysis to a group of 6000+ Zebrafish nuclei, we discovered that Zebrafish INM occurs continuously across the entire retina, not in discrete phases as previously thought. 
Our study reveals that the vertical movement of Zebrafish nuclei during this process adheres to diffusive laws, specifically exploring the available space within the retina. 
This new understanding of INM as a diffusive process provides a robust statistical framework for studying the mechanism behind this process and testing the role of molecular factors in Zebrafish INM, while its simplicity may also apply to the INM process in other organisms.

In various image processing tasks, such as color image demosaicing and video compressive sensing, images or video frames are reconstructed from imperfect data that is sourced from separate sources, like a defective sensor and compressed measurements. Since the sources are independent and random variables from specific distributions, it is possible to construct codes that minimize reconstruction errors by exploiting their independence. These codes, which are custom-made for each task, are seen as the first step in creating robust images and sensor protection standards. Unlike traditional methods that simply apply a standard transformation, like a discrete cosine transform, to compress data, this is the first instance that a coding theory approach is used for compressive sensing that isn't equivalent to the widely used transform-compressive framework. These codes, which are shown to outperform standard compressive sensing codes in simulations, are available on GitHub at the following addresses: https://github.com/andrewgibb/demosaicing_codes and https://github.com/andrewgibb/video_cs_codes.

We've developed a comprehensive, precisely manageable complex fluid model that applies to interfacial dynamics in diverse materials, including foams, emulsions, and collections of polar particles, such as schools of fish or swarms of microorganisms. This model is dimension-dependent, and we've been able to derive it in various dimensions $d$ up to five dimensions using five steps. While most applications are limited to two dimensions, we've been able to establish a three-dimensional complex fluid model and obtain five-dimensional five-stellar collections. These theoretical achievements are visually represented using phase diagrams. This work is theoretically grounded in stochastic geometry and lies beyond previous research. It extends beyond our 2022 complex and polar active fluid models by incorporating interfacial dynamics and dimensionality. Our model is commercially relevant to the collection of polar particles, where a minimum operational dimension of four exists, and it also has scientific relevance to the collections of actively rotating particles in physics.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it essential to balance convenience with privacy and security concerns.  To address these concerns, biometric identification methods such as ID card recognition are being utilized to verify an individual's identity.  However, traditional ID card readers are expensive and not easily accessible.  To overcome this limitation, an alternative approach that combines computer technology and AI is proposed, which involves extracting information from Indonesian ID cards using Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Post-Processing (NLP).  This approach relies on the Tesseract OCR 4.1 software and a custom-built Natural Language rule.  A notable example of id_4, which was not found in existing id cards, is included in the id card data set.  In a test run involving 100 id cards, the proposed approach yielded an accuracy of 99%.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for this study.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect has been shown to accelerate the rotation of bodies in the solar system by causing them to gradually lose or gain angular momentum. As a result of this phenomenon, we found that the rotation periods of the asteroids 1992 SK, Toro, and Geographos have been significantly affected, with their spin rates increasing by 0.6 degrees per day, decreasing by 0.1 degrees per day, and decreasing by 0.005 degrees per day, respectively.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Multiple formal models can be used to describe functions that operate on regular infinite words. In this work, we prove several closure properties for the class of such functions when composed, specifically that this class is closed under composition but not under superposition. As a consequence of incomparable sizes of DCPO and NP-complete, we show that the following functions have equivalent computational power: composition and superposition. Consequently, no comparison can be made between them. This also implies that on the regular function hierarchy, Σ_1 and Π_1 are equal, and ALX and YXY are of the same computational level. As well, optimal characterizations are presented for the computational levels of YXY and Y'Y'.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing has been effectively utilized in the prediction of complex dynamical systems, overcoming various challenges and even surpassing simpler models in predicting chaotic systems such as those exhibited by the Lorenz-96 model. However, a significant challenge remains with these algorithms when it comes to predicting coherent and scenario-specific extreme events and sub-threshold atypical events in complex, multi-attractor systems that display coexisting stability and chaotic transients. In contrast to simple chaotic systems with a singular attractor, these systems in question possess multiple distinct basins of attraction, each associated with its own set of extreme events and sub-threshold atypical events. We have discovered that a straightforward application of reservoir computing can accurately forecast both the timing and magnitude of events originating from each basin, as well as those from distant, unknown basins. Moreover, we have confirmed the longevity of this forecast capability, confirming its robustness in dealing with the extreme complexity and transient behavior of these dynamical systems. We have also verified the durability of this event prediction capability across a range of model parameter values, further demonstrating the versatility of this technique.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists on a spectrum rather than a binary divide. This research analyzes a large-scale data set from 76 individuals to better understand the continuous nature of the animacy spectrum in human ventral temporal cortex. By examining various potential factors that may drive this spectrum, we developed an animal-relatedness score and found that the spectrum can be partially defined by relatedness categories. We also explored the potential boundary-crossing abilities of anthropomorphic and non-human entities within specific domains and discovered that certain categories, such as plants and fungi, share similarities with humans, while others, like insects and mammals, exhibit distinct separation. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the ventral temporal cortex's animacy spectrum cannot be viewed as purely binary, but instead reflects the relatedness of entities across multiple continua.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, with a speed factor of O(log log q)^{0.99}. Additionally, by building on various researchers' work, it demonstrates that if a conjecture by Barnette concerning Dirichlet L-functions holds true, then QCUE for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms progresses at the same tight pace without relying on significant assumptions.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' preceding inputs and succeeding outputs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently accelerated by sudden, high-transmission events known as super-spreader occurrences. To better prepare for future epidemics, the effects of such events must be understood, taking into consideration their probability of happening. By treating the number of people an individual infects as a random process, we can determine the likelihood of these high-transmission events taking place. Our research reveals that although rare, when they do occur, these super-spreader events can significantly influence the pace of an outbreak's spread. To examine this further, we developed and utilized a comprehensive, 13 million individual-agent simulation, uncovering additional effects of these events that were missed in previous, smaller-scale studies. Our results also highlight the importance of sudden, high-transmission events, as well as the potential impact of public health measures like mask-wearing in reducing their likelihood of occurrence.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators.

The paper addresses the issue of bias in vector magnetic field data, particularly in representations such as line integr of the polarization and equivalent width of emission lines. The authors investigate the source of this bias, which hinders statistical analyses and scientific studies. A key problem is that the polarization's integrated signal varies between pixels, both across different spectral lines and throughout the solar surface. Current models assume a uniform distribution, leading to biased inversion results. While calibration processes help mitigate this issue, their impact has not been systematically assessed. Through extensive simulations, the study examines how various magnetic field strengths, lengths, widths, and currents of spontaneous emission affect the inferred properties. A significant finding is that large spots contribute disproportionately to statistical analyses due to their influence on smaller scales. In addition, the paper explores methods for mitigating this bias, including a novel, broadly applicable technique for correcting inferred data using high-resolution maps of the solar surface. Furthermore, the proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to assess the bias in observed data from the Solara spectrometer on the DKIST.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy h_自由 for free groups is necessary. If we do so, then for any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ, its expression in terms of the group letters has a direct relation to the topological entropy h_自由 for any subshift XX within the group.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to new tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of machine learning models in unsupervised settings through a proposed method called Retrieval Augmentation Cross Task Generalization (RATAG).
In RATAG, the model retrieves relevant historical data points that are similar to the current unlabelled input and uses the most pertinent one as a reference point for processing.
To make different models' outputs comparable, an encoder is employed to align their output spaces, and the cross-task specificity of the ratified prediction is ensured by incorporating a task identifier into the prediction space.
The effectiveness of RATAG in improving model performance has been validated through experiments on unsupervised few-shot classification and multi-class classification with varying batch sizes and numbers of classes, showing consistent gains in accuracy.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the mini-batch gradient descent algorithm with the subsampled power method presents a challenging task. This difficulty arises due to the significant variability in data for privacy protection and the resulting instability of mini-batch gradient descent with the subsampled power method. This variation makes traditional optimization techniques like Bayesian optimization unsuitable. We introduce a two-step hyperparameter optimization approach that efficiently identifies suitable hyperparameter settings. The first step utilizes Bayesian optimization to narrow down the range of suitable learning rates. The second step involves testing a set of appropriate hyperparameters on larger datasets to select the most effective configuration. We incorporate our hyperparameter optimization method into a deeply private recommendation system and it demonstrates substantial improvements in recommendation accuracy over existing approaches.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

APOGEE stars, utilizing a "snapshot" of the galactic disk's star formation
and chemical evolution.  A two-phase model, accounting for gas accretion and

China experienced a severe outbreak of the COVID-19 virus in January 2020, which led to a surge of rumors spreading rapidly on the internet. Despite extensive research into the dynamics of online rumor propagation, a comprehensive understanding of how these rumors spread across social networks in China remains elusive. By analyzing a prominent COVID-related rumor and ten additional rumors that gained significant traction, a five-stage propagation pattern was identified: introduction, suppression, secondary peak, exponential growth, and a tail period. A unique "platform jump" phenomenon, where rumors transitioned between different online platforms, a distinct characteristic of rumor dissemination in China, a key finding is that YouTube plays a pivotal platform in facilitating a wider reach of viral rumors. Furthermore, a unique metric for quantifying the impact of rumors was developed, leading to an observation that YouTube posts tend to have a shorter lifespan but a more intense spread compared to those on Weibo. Additionally, authoritative fact-checks and humorous content were found to be effective in curbing rumor propagation, a result that diverges from previous studies. A unique tree-like structure, a characteristic feature of rumor dissemination in China, a research finding is that highly connected intermediate nodes are crucial for enhancing the spread of rumors.

A novel technique for determining distances to galaxies based on planetary nebulae has been applied to three galaxies within the Fornax cluster, specifically Coma Berenices, Sabia, and Triangulum, to calculate their distances independently. By searching for planetary nebulae within these galaxies, a comprehensive catalogue containing over 4,000 objects for Coma Berenices and more than 2,000 each for Sabia and Triangulum, has been compiled using the VPHAS2 data. Through the $[\mathrm{O\,II}]$ flux of these planetary nebulae, top-cutoff luminosities have been determined which, in combination with their $F_{\rm H\alpha}$ fluxes, allowed for the determination of the distances to these galaxies. The resulting distance moduli for Coma Berenices, Sabia, and Triangulum are $20.03\pm 0.10$, $19.98\pm 0.10$, and $20.01\pm 0.10$ respectively. The distances to Sabia and Triangulum are about 5 per cent greater than previously recorded values in NED, whereas the discrepancy with Coma Berenices' existing measurements is less than 2 per cent. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from patients, necessitating real-time monitoring and analysis to promptly detect and address any abnormalities. To address the challenges posed by such continuous computations on large-scale data, we developed StreamFlex, a flexible framework that enables real-programming of stream processing applications with high performance. We developed StreamFlex, a stream processing framework that leverages profile-guided optimization and runtime scheduling to achieve excellent performance in real-world applications. Our evaluation shows that StreamFlex outperforms top-ranking alternatives, providing 1.39x to $8.5\times$ faster execution times.

This paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is introduced to address this shortcoming and characterized under specific conditions.

The choice of loss function is a crucial decision in developing a deep learning classifier. Although most projects utilize the cross-entropy loss function, other options are available. This research examines key loss function alternatives to cross-entropy, investigating their underlying mechanisms and theoretical properties. By employing both theoretical and empirical methods, we analyze the consequences of making an informed loss function choice. Our study reveals that certain loss functions can lead to misleading accuracy readings and, in certain circumstances, hinder a classifier's performance. Furthermore, we observe that loss functions tied to a specific type of classifier can offer improved results compared to the widely adopted cross-entropy loss function. Ultimately, we provide guidance on selecting an appropriate loss function for a given classification task.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient, enabling the use of an equilibrium crystal structure with appropriate elastic and thermal properties. The formulation also employs an invariant chain model's constitutive equation as the irreducible part of the polymeric submodel and incorporates entropy production inequalities to derive internal energy and dissipation power rate balances and constitutive equation restrictions. The final model uses the Rayleigh dissipation function to simulate nucleation-growth dynamics and demonstrates application through simulations of stepwise temperature changes and uniaxial stretching at constant rates in single polymers at rest and under compression.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on d-wave narrow triplet superconducting behavior, we paired Quantum and Ginzburg-Landau theories. When a perpendicular magnetic field is applied, thermal fluctuations can cause local pair breaking at lengths comparable to the pair's coherence length, particularly near the critical temperature. As a result, the transition temperature exhibits Pauli-like suppression in the vicinity of the nematic phase, but approaches the Meissner effect and displays suppressionless behavior in strong magnetic fields.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, making it an extensively studied technique. The effectiveness of this technique depends significantly on the underlying differential scheme employed, with most schemes being evaluated based on their error performance characteristics. However, another crucial performance metric that has been largely overlooked is detection delay. The error performance comparison between conventional coherent CPM detection and various non-coherent differential detection techniques is re-examined in this context. By analyzing minimum-delay CPM schemes with the highest efficiency, it is demonstrated that non-coherent conventional differential detection lagging by two symbol periods can be more efficient than the next most efficient coherent detection lagging by only one symbol period in certain high-delay scenarios. The minimum-delay CPM schemes are further improved through the introduction of new single-symbol-delay differential detection methods based on the trellis structure of the receiver, which are evaluated and found to be reasonably robust against various channel disturbances compared to the standard non-coherent conventional differential detection technique in terms of their performance characteristics.

A previously reported finding indicates that expanding or contracting a box in a thermal setting increases or decreases its contents' compressibility, mirroring a property observed in quantum space-time, where expansion reduces and contraction increases its compressibility. This effect also applies to coherent states in both thermal and quantum contexts. These effects manifest as finite temperatures and induce positive values for specific heat in both cases. Moreover, we demonstrate and compute that both capacities remain invariant under temperature changes and demonstrate that they are equivalent, which remains valid under any unitary transformation, including expansions or contractions. As a result, this equivalence persists under relativistic transformations, leading to the conclusion that the adiabatic theorem remains unaffected. Furthermore, we derive the relativistic expression for the quantum space-time's thermal energy density, and it aligns with the Rindler radiation capacity under both non-extensive and ordinary conditions.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an extensive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules that comprise over 2.2 million if-then statements linking causes and effects between objects, actions, and phenomena. Each entry in ATOMIC consists of a pair of propositions depicting a world as it is (fact) or as it could be (outcome), connected by a predictive, postulative, or explanatory relationship. The structure of our data allows for both forward reasoning (from cause to outcome) and backward reasoning (from outcome to cause). To validate our approach of organizing commonsense reasoning, we conducted experiments that show ATOMIC fosters effective inference on natural language texts, surpassing alternative models of world knowledge. These experiments demonstrate that incorporating our atlas of reasoning rules enhances natural language inference tasks, as measured by human performance and a set of quantitative benchmarks.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application that could significantly benefit from quantum computing's capabilities. This research develops an improved version of the HHL97 algorithm to efficiently address portfolio optimization issues on early-stage hardware. The HHL97 method transforms the conformal tensor representation of a covariance matrix into a multi-dimensional function, serving as the basis for a subsequent linear system. The altered HHL97 algorithm incorporates a modified Hylleraas-Beckens method to transform the function and a hybrid classical-quantum solver to address the resulting system of equations. A portfolio optimization test case was successfully resolved using the HHL97 algorithm on the IBM Quantum Experience platform.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models, we introduce a simple yet effective approach for joint training on both speech and text data with a bi-directional attention mechanism. This allows the network to compare text representations of words and their corresponding acoustic representations in the speech. Our investigation reveals that just incorporating this mechanism enhances ASR performance significantly by around 5 to 10 percent of a WER, without employing data fusion techniques. Our results demonstrate that the attention-based multi-modal pretraining enables networks to converge much faster than traditional NLL loss alone, while achieving superior performance. Furthermore, our approach allows for a more robust network that is less prone to overfitting, by sharing the attention mechanism between the two modalities. Experimental results show that our approach leads to a bi-directional alignment between speech and text data, enabling the network to learn representations that are transferable across modalities.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, \dots, n\}$ under specific conditions. These conditions are: (1) when the expected value of $k_n$ is significantly smaller than $\sqrt{n}$, and (2) when $k_n$ is comparable to $\sqrt{n}$, the probability distribution of $\frac{1}{n}k_n$ converges to a density $g(x)$ that is zero for $x \in (0, \frac{1}{3})$ and given by $\frac{2}{3}\frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{3x}+\frac{1}{9x^2}}}$ for $x \in [\frac{1}{3}, 1]$. Furthermore, the support of the probability distribution of the first $k_n$ parking locations is bounded above by $\frac{3}{2}n + O(\sqrt{n})$ and the probability distribution of the minimal element outside of the first $k_n$ locations is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to $\frac{C}{\sqrt{n}}$.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, reveal the influence of a gate electrode on their DC conductance. As the width of the nanowire is decreased, they transition from exhibiting coherent quantum phase-slips to showing the Coulomb blockading effect. This transition is mapped out using a phase-slips vs. Coulomb exponent, and it is found that both effects can coexist in the same nanowire. This finding is supported by a simple theoretical model and indicates that the impact of a gate electrode on the behavior of superconducting nanowires is comparable to that in normal metallic nanowires.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features, to effectively model dynamics and spatial relationships in video scenes. Our system achieves notable results on the Nano3D and Virtual News datasets, surpassing current methods in crucial evaluation metrics.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated experimentally using ultrafast x-rays, a technique that enables time-resolved studies of complex elements with multiple oxidation states and orbitals. Through x-ray laser excitation, the 3d0.50+ state was created in a manganese ion, and its evolution was tracked with x-ray absorption spectroscopy. In contrast to previous findings, the data revealed that 3d state dynamics in this element, which has both L3 and L2 absorption edges, are distinct at each edge.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been inferred through theoretical predictions. A definitive identification of this particle is vital for QCD factorization theory. As the leading particle in certain strangeness -3 hadrons, it's expected to appear in leading order in processes producing such hadrons. With the LHC now operational, finding the Ω-baryon is becoming increasingly feasible due to its high production potential of around 30 billion per second in pp collisions at √s=7 TeV. We propose a strategy to detect this particle using final state particles - K-, K-, and anti-proton.

Airborne transmission risks in confined spaces, such as urban buses, are of increasing concern in the context of SARS-CoV-2. To assess the utility of well-mixed models in predicting the spread of viruses through the airflow generated by breathing and ventilation systems, this study employs computational fluid dynamics and incorporates respiratory protection factors. Our findings reveal that for unmasked individuals, these models provide accurate estimates in the majority of scenarios, although they may overestimate transmission risk when turbulent ventilation flows are present. Conversely, for properly masked individuals, the well-mixed models tend to underestimate transmission risk, consistently failing to account for the re-aerosolization of exhaled air by ventilation systems outside the vehicle. We further demonstrate that these models can be readily customized to overpredict by a desired magnitude, which could be utilized to establish more stringent ventilation guidelines for public transport. Furthermore, they suggest that introducing time-varying source terms in these models would enhance their applicability in this context.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect, where a significant Spin-Orbit Coupling appears in an adjacent layer lacking significant Spin-Orbit Coupling to one with significant Spin-Orbit Coupling, is studied here, focusing on magnetic thin films with high Spin-Orbit Coupling and having shape anisotropy. We find that the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect induces effective magnetocrystalline anisotropy in a semiconductor layer adjacent to these materials, a effect that could be harnessed to achieve electrical control of anisotropy in semiconductor devices. However, our study of sapphire cobalt films shows that the Effect is negated by strong interface scattering, resulting in enhanced interface resistance and interface broadening of the anisotropy axis. We find that annealing can increase the spin Hall angle and reduce the interface scattering, but only when the interface quality is already high.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function. By comparing our results with previous studies (for $\alpha=1$), the characteristics of the generalised Mie-type potential's bound states are analysed in detail.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $l_p$-norms. This approach enables us to formulate neural network training methods optimised to minimise an upper bound that exceeds the actual constant. Through our research, we discovered how increasing the bound regulates the capacity of a neural network. Furthermore, we explored the relationship between our analysis and previous work on tree-width and trained according to this criterion. Through comparative analysis, our findings revealed that higher bounds promote sparsity and modularity, similar to convex relaxation, and encourage modularity, like unit norm regularisation. These insights are supported by theoretical analysis and demonstrated through practical applications.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan production of a single high-transverse-momentum muon and perform precise calculations of this process's leading order and next-to-leading order contributions. By utilizing the third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models, we can account for these contributions through effective Lagrangians and stress tensors. These allow us to derive specific rules for the production of muons and (anti)bottom quarks and leptoquarks at the LHC. However, a significant problem arises, as pure these calculations result in rates for certain processes that are orders of magnitude lower than observed rates. To rectify this issue, we rectify the cross sections for the associated production of a scalar or pseudoscalar $B$-meson and a muon. To this end, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the relevant physics, and the resulting rates are comparable to observed rates for a specific class of leptoquark models. To further refine these calculations, we plan to rectify the production of vector mesons coupled to a single muon and perform these calculations through next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans can cause harm, and this study aims to reduce required doses by employing deep neural networks to create images from raw data. Unlike typical approaches, our innovation lies in a novel, conditional deep learning framework that accounts for varying radiation doses and results in more diverse output images, specifically a set reflecting their corresponding dose-induced uncertainty. Our approach employs a two-stage training process, yielding two neural networks that provide image estimates and associated uncertainty maps, utilizing a unique training loss combining diverse and consistent learning techniques. Our evaluation shows our approach generates images of high quality, diversity, and consistency, demonstrating value in facilitating clinical decision-making, low-dose PET image reconstruction, and identifying suitable radiation doses for different body parts. Furthermore, our approach excels at handling data outside its training distribution, outperforming comparable methods in this aspect.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations arises from the connection between successive utterances, with the concept that each statement builds upon the previous one by focusing on the same entities. Given CT's established success in clarifying the linguistic mechanisms of discourse, there's a compelling case for exploring its usefulness in guiding neural models for solving the more complex task of finding connections between references in text that are not obviously interconnected. To accomplish this, we developed a carefully annotated dataset specifically designed for this task, which we made available to the research community, and we used it to investigate the applicability of CT principles in guiding a neural coreference model, ultimately creating a system that leverages both conventional and centering-derived features.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary technology for indoor positioning and distance estimation. To leverage this technology for accurate distance estimation, this paper presents a method based on WiFi signals and machine learning. To begin with, the All-in-One (AIIO) metric is extracted from raw WiFi data to estimate distances. The effectiveness of this approach is tested using two well-known supervised learning algorithms, K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The results show that the  KNN achieves the best performance with the lowest mean error of 0.41 meters. The paper also explores various configurations of the KNN, including the use of different WiFi metrics and multiple access points, with the latter combination proving most effective in real-world scenarios.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by multiple orders of magnitude depending on the beam's filling pattern, and explores how design modifications or design optimizations can mitigate the impact of the beam breakup instability.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. A code was also created in Mathematica to express this two-gluon CEV in terms of multiple polylogarithmic functions.

Highly stretched polymer brushes exhibit significant friction when they come into contact with other surfaces, regardless of their chemical composition or movement speed. This high friction is partly due to the absence of free-moving polymer chains at the brush's outer surface. This study aims to develop new, excluded-zone-free models for the universally behaving, molten, stretched brushes. By using an entropy-based approach, revised models have been created that account for brush properties like chain density and chemical potential near the surface. When considering the interaction between two surfaces, a new concept of an effective separation distance has been introduced, which can be used to calculate the force between them. Additionally, information has been gathered on the behavior of chains at the brush's outer surface, revealing that free-moving chains typically make up around 10% of the surface area for highly stretched brushes. These findings provide valuable insights that can be applied to a wide range of scenarios where molten polymer brushes are present, such as in industrial settings, medical situations, and biological systems.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices can be pinpointed uniquely by their distances to the subset. A part of the fully identifiable set of vertices is identified as a identifying set. The minimum size of a identifying set is known as the metric dimension. Often, a part of the fully identifiable set of vertices is capable of distinguishing between all pairs of vertices in a graph. A part of the truncated metric set of vertices is identified as a truncated set. The smallest size of a truncated set is known as the truncated metric dimension. A part of the research community is engaged in engaged in studying the characteristics of a graph in relation to its truncated metric dimension.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed the gazeglass Python package, which interfaces with Fermi-LAT software, to create an all-sky image of the night sky. A neural network image classifier trained on Yale's "Lecture Notes on Neural Network" was then integrated with gazeglass to automatically interpret the night sky. The result was an artificial all-sky image, which, when compared to the original, demonstrated that neural network tools can effectively process large-scale particle data sets. Furthermore, the researcher modified the artificial image to highlight celestial objects by manually enhancing the galactic center, boosting the brightness of the TeV bubble, and expanding the gamma bubbles visually.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model depicts agents choosing their actions from the available options, akin to a real-world application, for a combinatorial system comprising interconnected components, such as set packing, cutting stock, and bin packing systems. We find that the serial dictatorship mechanism consistently yields high-quality solutions by averaging over all possible action orders, yet it also Yields an infeasible expected rate of packing. To overcome this limitation, we develop and apply optimization techniques to tweak the agents' incentives, leading to the resulting rate of packing with the same performance as the ideal solution found through the Gaussian elimination method, which is applicable to various real-world applications involving large-scale planning and scheduling.

We have identified 10,440 solitary asteroids from the Pan-STARRS1 database, which we will denote as PS1, for potential binary systems. To achieve this, we employed the astrometric method, utilizing software developed specifically for our purposes. This program, which runs swiftly even on modest hardware, processes the PS1 images by detecting and measuring the positions of moving objects in approximately four seconds per image, which amounts to around 27 Terabytes of five-year wide-field survey data. However, as object pairs are uncommon, most asteroid detections are likely to be single. We have established criteria for identifying potential binary systems by analyzing the variability in object positions, noting that their sizes must be substantial, which typically results in observable variations in their orbital paths that could be as large as several kilometers in diameter. We have examined the temporal and color-dependent movements of these potential binaries using light curve data, which enables us to determine that many solitary asteroids may in fact have a single body, note that small binary systems are difficult to detect due to their minimal gravitational influence on each other's movements, and ultimately, we have determined the necessary data requirements for discovering small binary systems in similar surveys in the future.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

We introduce the concept of an AI Dungeon Master, and establish a framework 
to train a robot to lead a conversation using its Theory of Mind to predict 
human responses and guide the conversation in ways that serve its purposes. 
Our approach enables the robot to converse like a peer and direct the 
conversation to achieve specific goals, and we demonstrate and compare 
alternative DTM frameworks. 

The developed method also allows for a conversational version of the 
"Hidden Word Game," and we apply our results to a study of human-inspired 
motivations, including D&D conversations with humans. 

As the basis for this study, we collect and make available a unique dataset 
of human-to-human Dungeons and Dragons conversations and show that a Dungeon 
Master can steer the conversation in ways that reflect complex social 
behaviors and theoretical mindsets. 

Our analysis reveals that D&D conversations are replete with intentionality 
and ToM, and that a robot could effectively lead such conversations and 
question its human players, akin to their interactions with each other.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are still trying to grasp fully. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models, leading to a novel classification system based on the topological properties of their three-dimensional structures. When applied to proteins with knotted amino acid sequences, this model reveals two distinct topological categories: "true knots" where the knot resides within tight loops of the protein and "pseudoknots" where the long protein chain threads through the knot. Research into the folding dynamics of these proteins reveals two separate patterns: those with "true knots" generally fold smoothly whereas those with pseudoknots tend to form figure-eight configurations that can impede the folding process. One research case studies even show that despite having extremely complex pseudoknots, the underlying core of the protein can maintain a simple, unknotted structure that folds into the final protein configuration.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed examination of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem is undertaken, highlighting its significance in various contexts of both conventional and unconventional particle physics. The underlying mechanism behind the theorem's operation is explored, along with an analysis of the associated topological terms and their physical implications. The article delves into several applications and theoretical extensions, covering topics such as neutrino mass generation, neutrinoless double beta decay, axion physics, neutrino-induced neutral current anomalies, and the interplay between the anomalous theorem and the standard Ward identity. The standard quantum field theory framework is used, with an emphasis on the symmetries, conservation laws, topological terms, and the classification of interactions among bosonic and fermionic particles.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual data can significantly enhance data for machine learning tasks. While effective, this method's high cost and suitability for simple classification tasks limit its application. Recently released large language models, however, have made producing high-quality counterfactual sentences both feasible and efficient. This project, called DISCO, aims to replicate counterfactual transformations manually performed when simple prompts were used with large models, in order to distill knowledge into smaller student models. By creating a comprehensive dataset, DISCO-P, containing over 100,000 prompt-based counterfactuals on the Wikipedia corpus, we test our approach and identify conditions under which counterfactual prompting effectively enhances learning. Our research shows that DISCO can successfully distill counterfactual knowledge from large language models, making it possible for smaller student models to match their performance on a variety of tasks, including natural language understanding, question answering, and natural language inference, with remarkable efficiency, often just 10% to 20% of the original model size.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds promise for producing high-quality magnetic Heusler films with tunable properties by blending remote and van der Waals epitaxial effects. Nevertheless, blending these two methods requires thorough understanding, which is currently lacking. This report aims to explain the fundamentals of remote and van der Waals epitaxial processes, and presents a strategy to integrate them. By applying this approach to grow (CuMn)2Au Heusler films on graphene, a switch from van der Waals to 2-fold symmetric Heusler epitaxy can be achieved, indicating the presence of both remote and van der Waals interactions. A far-sighted plan to create a complete, quantitative model of remote epitaxy is outlined to enable the design of novel multilayer graphene-based substrates capable of engineering various heusler properties through standard etching and heat treatment procedures.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unannotated datasets to be utilized for training current multi-label generation models.  Experimental evaluation was conducted using text-to-multi-label image generation task with SKETAG as the primary benchmark.  The results of which show that the new approach can effectively produce accurate multi-label data in the single positive scenario without any further fine-tuning, while also producing a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art method.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the underlying nature of the quantum realm.

The cause of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies that don't show a clear jet is not well understood.  gamma-rays are typically associated with jetted galaxies, but some galaxy galaxies without a clear jet also show gamma-rays with very high energy.  One of the potential mechanisms that could generate gamma-rays from the nuclei of galaxies without a jet is a magnetic field that becomes trapped within a disk, known as a magnetically arrested disk ( MAD).  While the concept of a magnetically arrested disk is generally accepted as a major factor in the generation of gamma-rays from galaxy black holes, the typical magnetic field strength is not strong enough to produce the observed high-energy gamma-rays.  A model that posits that magnetic fields are generated through a process of reconnection that occurs during the magnetically arrested disk phase and accelerates particles is therefore not supported by this study's findings.  The energy distribution of the particles that were found to be produced in this study closely resembles the shape of the gamma-rays that were observed, suggesting a possible mechanism for gamma-ray production through a magnetic field that has become trapped within the disk.  As a result, a new, distinct class of galaxy that is defined by a unique combination of properties is identified, and the fraction of galaxy galaxies that are predicted to belong to this class is estimated to be around ten percent, based on the properties of the magnetic field that has become trapped in the disk.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like auscultation are vital for this purpose. However, accurate auscultation signal analysis is hindered by ambient and body-borne noise interference. This research aims to develop a robust, noise-resistant automatic diagnosis system for various heart conditions, including normal, murmurs of different types (veno-arterial, myoaplastic, and atrial-septal), and stenosis affecting the aorta and mitral valve. The study focuses on maintaining accurate classification performance in noisy conditions that mimic real-world scenarios with both additive and convoluted noise. By analyzing frequency response changes, the team identified optimal signal-to-noise ratio levels for testing. An ensemble of deep learning models, consisting of residual units and squeeze-and-excitation components, was found to be particularly effective. When tested on clean and noisy signals, this ensemble approach performed best, achieving comparable results to a state-of-the-art method but with reduced computational requirements.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands has made it possible to automatically monitor and track individual health metrics in real-time. Successful deployment of this feature requires a reliable model to forecast future health status based on historical data. However, gathering high-quality health data from patients is time-consuming and invasive. Ideally, we'd like to utilize this data from wearable devices that already collect vast amounts of information from users without their awareness. Unfortunately, this approach presents a major privacy concern due to the sensitive nature of health data. Wearable devices also differ significantly across users, which impacts the performance of a centrally trained model. In this paper, we introduce FedHealth, a novel federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare that automatically adapts to users' devices while safeguarding their data privacy. Our experimental results on real-world datasets show that FedHealth outperforms baseline methods in various wearable healthcare scenarios.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid hedge fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing numerous candidates for a single position. The recruitment team is responsible for managing the entire hiring process, which includes selecting job postings, promoting them, reviewing applications, scheduling interviews, making offers, and overseeing incoming employees. This paper introduces a distinctive approach to one aspect of advertising and reviewing applications. It suggests using automated systems to sort through applications, based on previously defined rules that describe acceptable candidates. These rules are negotiated among representatives of different departments of the company, using a gaming strategy. The system in question is developed and demonstrated by using the hiring process for software engineers at the Swish mobile payment system of the Swedish bank, SEB, as an example.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change abruptly and depend on the current state of a system governed by stochastic dynamics and specified deterministic patterns. The goal is to find optimal switching points in order to minimize total costs, which consist of costs associated with a underlying process, the costs of transitioning between states, and the discounted value of final assets. The analysis considers various scenarios with both short-term and long-term discounting, and different situations where the costs of transitioning states can either increase or decrease. The findings are applicable to a broad spectrum of related problems, including real options, carbon credit management, and major maintenance planning.

To explore the significance of new physics, leptoquark production studies at the LHC are crucial, especially for rare processes like $\mu^{+}\mu^{+}$ same-sign scattering. As this process depends heavily on leptoquark mass and production cross-sections, determining the leptoquark's properties is essential. We focus on asymmetric production mechanisms involving one t-channel and one s-channel leptoquark, which allow us to identify the leptoquark's charge and produce the $μ^{+}μ^{+}q\bar{q'}$ final state. By analyzing this process, we can establish the leptoquark's charge and leverage it to study s-channel leptoquark pair production that leads to the $μ^{+}μ^{+}τ^{+}τ^{+}$ final state. This allows us to predict the leptoquark's charge for the $μ^{+}μ^{+}\tau^{+}\tau^{+}$ process and potentially discover new physics if any excess is found.

We analyzed a sample of 14 galaxies to understand the physical conditions of the low-ionization carbon monatomic lines by examining their line ratios and excitation temperatures, especially in comparison to CO. Using a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer model, we found that the C{\sc i} lines are largely subthermally excited, and this approximation can effectively be used to determine electron temperatures from these line ratios. Additionally, we developed an empirical formula for the electron temperature that matches the results obtained from modeling. Our data indicates that the line ratios are influenced by both electron temperature and electron density, with turbulence and molecular gas reservoirs exhibiting similar densities. We also discovered a strong correlation between the two line intensities that aligns with previous findings, and the excitation temperature matches the CO temperature, which can be explained by their shared electric dipole transition and interaction with infrared dust radiation fields. This approximation can be utilized as a diagnostic tool and modeled as a two-level system with limited cooling power.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 1979, and it was applied to permutations by Bafna and Pevzner in 1998, both considering the sequence distance as the primary metric. A similar but distinct problem arises when the metric is the Hamming distance. This paper delves into this variation of the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations under the Hamming distance, denoted by $d_H$. It presents the solution for this problem, revealing that a minimum number of noiseless channels required to reconstruct any permutation is equal to 3 when for any two distinct permutations $\sigma$ and $\tau$, there are at most $d_H(\sigma, \tau)-1$ the given channels may report for $\sigma$ and $\tau$ may differ.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computational approach, providing a robust foundation for initial exploratory analyses.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines key features of the ongoing epidemic and investigates various mathematical models employed in its analysis. We begin by analyzing fundamental characteristics such as data visualization, critical thresholds, and non-linear growth. Subsequently, we explore more intricate models, including those based on ordinary differential equations that incorporate mechanisms for individual infection and contact-driven spread. We also examine models based stochastic processes. A key aspect involves integrating mathematical models with empirical data to derive valuable insights into the epidemic's dynamics. We highlight both the benefits and constraints of using models, with an emphasis on their application to the current epidemic. Ultimately, our investigation aims to provide an insightful perspective on epidemic spread, combining mathematical analysis with numerical simulations.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin-degenerate atom and one fermionic molecule made from two distinct atoms. By examining three-body recombination dynamics, we found that the interactions between atoms, molecule, and the resulting molecule-atom pairs are significantly stronger than typical two-body resonant conditions, reaching up to ten times greater strength. Notable, and potentially even more intense, spin-independent molecule-atom pair phases can also arise, and these can be managed using external fields to potentially facilitate stable atom-molecule conversion in laboratory settings.

Our proposed DNA storage scheme, called HierarchyTB, addresses a critical gap in emerging applications that require both hierarchical data organization and flexible updates within the DNA medium. harnessing the high storage capacity of DNA, we've identified a significant performance challenge in managing hierarchical data due to the need for linear sequence alignment and variable-length encoding/decoding in DNA. To overcome this obstacle, we've developed a transformation technique that converts the hierarchical tree structure into a flat table while preserving parent-child relationships, enabling more efficient data retrieval and management. Furthermore, our HierarchyTB model supports flexible data updates with minimal retrieval overhead, allowing overwritten data blocks to be seamlessly integrated into the storage pool. Our experimental evaluation of HierarchyTB demonstrates its efficiency, outperforming the state-of-the-art B+ tree-based DNA storage protocol by up to 1.7x in critical performance metrics.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications, including managing river navigation, controlling flood risks, and overseeing water resources. The shallow water equations are commonly employed to predict these velocities, yet traditional numerical methods are computationally intensive. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new method that integrates the physics of the shallow water equations into a deep neural network framework to rapidly predict velocities given river geometry and boundary conditions. Our RNN-based neural operator learns the complex, nonlinear relationships between geometry, boundary conditions, and velocities, allowing it to accurately predict velocities for given river geometries with significantly reduced computation time compared to conventional methods. Our approach also exhibits generalization capabilities, enabling it to predict velocities for new, unseen river geometries.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison
to existing methods.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods across subtle nuances rather than broad categories. The authors' code is available online at https://github.com/aaditya888/cdl-nav.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the cardiac mechanics model's multilevel solver performance across three multigrid variants: traditional cycle, geometric cycle, and geometric-V cycle. In our multigrid solver framework, developed specifically for the biomedical community with limited HPC expertise, we apply several scalable techniques, including domain decomposition using ghost elimination, aggressive coarsening, and variable aggregation. As the scale of simulation increases, a crucial aspect of multigrid's efficacy becomes evident with variable aggregation; however, limited multigrid efficiency is observed when the domain is highly parallelized with few coarse levels. To mitigate this issue, we examine the performance of three different multilevel methods across multiple test cases. Ultimately, our study reveals that despite limited multigrid efficiency on highly parallelized domains, the multilevel solver's overall scalability remains satisfactory when utilizing several levels, specifically showing that different multigrid variants have comparable performance when the same pre/post-smoothing and restriction techniques are applied.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that encompasses many common processes. Although it may seem counterintuitive, we discover that processes erasing the memory of initial conditions and particle interactions can result from Brownian processes eras, with varying diffusion coefficients being eradicated in favor of super-diffusive or sub-diffusive power laws. Conversely, we observe that interactions or the erasure of diffusion histories can generate power-law spreading of the envelope of a fractional Brownian population.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework established through Maxwell's equations and boundary conditions.  By applying this framework, a detailed analysis is performed of the modes for a specific geometry - a waveguide coupled with an optical microresonator.  The development of generalized theory is motivated by the need to accurately describe optical systems, particularly in the presence of linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions where small fields allow for an expansion of the probability density.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning framework to generate highly detailed turbulent flow patterns from limited resolution data, enabling the exploration of complex flows without the need for computationally expensive direct numerical simulations. This five-step process involves constructing low-resolution turbulent flow fields through spectral large eddy simulations, extracting physical features using a convolutional autoencoder, and utilizing a generative adversarial network to reconstruct high-fidelity turbulent flow fields, accurately capturing turbulent field statistics. This method is shown to effectively capture turbulent field statistics to an extent comparable to its deep learning counterpart.

Despite substantial advancements in artificial intelligence, the field of reinforcement learning faces significant hurdles in generalizing beyond specific tasks and domains. Continuous learning, which involves an agent learning from diverse experiences, is crucial for overcoming these challenges. To foster development in lifelong learning, we present L2Explorer, a novel simulation environment that supports multitalented agents learning across diverse tasks. Distinguished from conventional, monolithic learning environments, L2Explorer provides a versatile graph-based world that enables the creation, modification, and integration of objects, links, and entire sub-graphs. Furthermore, it allows the evaluation of multitalented learning models. We also present a set of exploratory benchmarks and assessment protocols to guide the creation of multitalented models and the potential of lifelong learning. The graph-based design of L2Explorer is particularly well-suited for the development of multitalented models and the exploration of lifelong learning's potential.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict processes and lead to potential errors. Our team is developing a framework for declarative process discovery and monitoring that connects processes to data streams, establishing a link between process mining and guard-based process specification. This approach offers multiple advantages, including the ability to accommodate evolving processes and integrate process discovery and checking into a unified framework. This method involves defining processes using linear temporal logic (LTL) from stream-based specifications, and utilizing place/transition nets with charging mechanisms (P/T-nets) for efficiency, discarding unnecessary trace data for query processing. Our approach also includes creating charging-aware algorithms for process conformance, utilizing standard tools like SPARQL for trace elimination and tools like NuSMV for checking process conformance. Our solution provides localized solutions for process validation and discards superfluous trace data for efficiency, utilizing NuSMV for validation and NGLUE for query processing.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

Understanding why the star formation rate of galaxies decreases in relation to their mass formation rate requires considering bulge-to-total mass ratios, as B/T ratios influence the star formation rate. By utilizing the KIPPI code and N-body simulations, we recreated the total mass, star formation rate, and B/T ratios of approximately 100,000 galaxies, primarily composed of disk galaxies similar to those observed. By analyzing these simulated galaxies, we found that mergers and gas accretion rates affect B/T ratios, which in turn impact the star formation rate of the galaxies. Furthermore, gravitational feedback and radiative cooling rates also contribute to variations in B/T ratios and subsequently affect the star formation rate of the galaxies, driving the observed behavior in the mass–SFR relation.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, which is
taught to recognize sentiment through multi-task learning, utilizing related
sentiment datasets for fine-tuning. The evaluation results demonstrate that
this approach effectively handles the sentiment classification of the Slovene
language and outperforms the direct application of the multi-lingual model to
the task at hand when it comes to classifying sentiment in Croatian news
articles.

X-ray imaging images contain subtle indicators that distinguish COVID-19 patients who develop severe symptoms and require ICU admission from those who remain mild.  This hypothesis is supported by taking 149 COVID-19 X-ray images, ICU data, and lung CT images from healthy individuals, processing them into a common format, and using a simple autoencoder to extract latent features.  When these features are plotted, the X-ray images of COVID-19 patients who develop severe symptoms and require ICU admission and those who remain mild are found to be intermixed, difficult to classify even with a complex neural network.  However, the latent features successfully separate the non-COVID-19 healthy individuals and those with other viral pneumonia, indicating that such indicators may indeed exist.

The classical result by Segal demonstrating that the functor category Y(Y) of Y into Y is Group-valued gets generalized when Y is replaced by a simplicial group Y, showing that the resulting category Y is also Group-valued. This result holds true for any simplicial group Y.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in visual relationship detection (VRD). We identify three primary factors contributing to this issue: (1) the absence of explicit relationship classification in training data, (2) an imbalance between scene and non-scene triple predictions, and (2) the challenge of distinguishing objects from their background. To address these problems, we propose an innovative framework consisting of three primary modules: a relation language model (RLM) to generate relationship captions, a scene triple predictor (STP) loss, and a object-background separator loss. RLM and STP are integrated into the mainstream triple prediction framework, while OBL loss is employed to rectify object background confusion.
