In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated for the setting of Holoberger-Schwartz distributions on locally convex spaces. To achieve this, we establish the key property that integration commutes with partial differentiation in this context. Additionally, we re-examine the situation when the domain of integration is compact, demonstrating how the Stokes formula simplifies in this scenario. To develop the necessary foundations for this work, we examine the properties of differential forms for infinite-dimensional spaces, providing explicit definitions and examining their structural properties.

Autonomous navigation for unmanned surface vehicles in unknown environments is
challenging due to the need for real-time map updates, obstacle avoidance, and
path planning. This paper presents a novel approach that combines sonar depth
sensing with a layered navigation controller to enable unmanned surface vehicles
to operate independently in unknown environments. The proposed system allows
the vehicle to create a simple map of its surroundings, follow a predefined
path, and follow a predefined path while avoiding obstacles in real-time using
separate navigation layers. Each layer has a specific purpose and is passed
along to the next one if its task is completed. The results show that the
proposed control system is effective in guiding an unmanned surface vehicle
through an unknown environment.

The prevalence of false news on the internet is a significant issue, with consequences that can be severe. Due to the amount of information required to verify authenticity, humans struggle to effectively process online content. This project aims to utilize automatic text summarization to identify false news by leveraging its structural characteristics. If such models can successfully approximate the algorithmic nature of self-generated news aggregators, even simple machine learning models can potentially achieve their goal. Our research builds upon the work of (Yu 2018), which discovered that employing the average sentence length and tree-structure based text simplification yielded better results than utilizing simply-derived summaries for their intended purpose.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' geometry. The results revealed an interesting phenomenon known as a "curvature effect," where the models exhibited significant nonlinear patterns due to an intrinsic relationship between the model's parameters and data in complex space. The curvature effect hinders accurate local modeling and suggests that linear modeling techniques may be limited in their applicability to certain systems.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data has served as the foundation for machine learning advancements. Nevertheless, the reliance on annotated data is constrained by supply limitations, particularly in machine-learning applications requiring sophisticated models like BERT. To bridge this gap, news articles with corresponding queries were divided into two components: part that carries explicit emotional content and part that is neutral. The emotional component was assumed to be annotated accurately due to their inherently emotional nature, while the neutral part was annotated as mislabelled with a fake emotion. Consequently, the neutral part was treated as unannotated content. By leveraging the emotional part's precise annotations, we aimed to BERT-assist in categorizing the Bunch of Amsterdams Emotion-Related Questies (BAERQ) dataset and other similar large-scale unannotated content. The result of this process yielded a specific sub-set of BAERQ that was effectively classified, while the rest of the content remained unannotated. This could be further utilized by the emotion research community as a robust benchmark or as a prime example of utilizing BERT to semantically annotate unsorted content.

For mobile robots to navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having a clear understanding of the environment is crucial for effective path planning. Current methods for representing environments from sensor data often focus on using local maps, which can hinder efficient navigation in complex settings with many potential routes. While global map representations, such as grid maps and graph-based maps, offer more efficient spatial understanding, they struggle with certain aspects, including dynamic obstacles and the loss of information during odometry integration. To overcome these limitations, we propose HiTMap, a novel method for representing space that combines hierarchical 2D landmark maps, which efficiently describe complex environments by integrating multiple local maps, optimizing path planning for navigation in unknown settings.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a particle undergoes free fall between mirrored mirrors via upward and downward movement, it experiences the Lorentz force due to local magnetic field expulsion from a superconducting plate, thereby inducing a phase shift. By comparing this shift to an unaffected atomic reference, it is possible to infer the magnitude of the expelled local magnetic field. By utilizing substantial mass and vertical distance in comparable experiments, scientists aim to further refine measurements by accounting for gravitational effects, ultimately seeking to pinpoint the Planck mass precision.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD architectures like GPUs has been limited by
object-oriented programming due to frequent memory allocation failures and
efficient memory access challenges.  To overcome these obstacles, we developed
DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator specifically designed for object-oriented
programs that can operate at high speed on SIMD GPUs.  DynaSOAr achieves
efficient memory access by reserving a contiguous memory block for each CPU
thread, eliminating the need for pointer chasing.  It also employs a content-addressed
hash table to accelerate lookups of object attributes.  To ensure reliable operation,
DynaSOAr uses a set of data structures that automatically adapt to changes in memory
usage.  Our performance tests show that DynaSOAr outperforms existing allocator
alternatives, scaling effectively to a large number of CPU threads and providing
significantly more available memory for applications using Fortran with OOP.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an ab inity treatment of the local magnetic moment within a non-equilibrium Green's function approach. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers situated on the Nb(110) surface. The calculated spin-resolved YSR state spectra are in agreement with the experimental data previously obtained. Additionally, a direct correlation has been identified between the spin polarization and the integral of the YSR state inside the atomic site. The level of spin polarization is found to be intimately linked to the level of local magnetization integral, which is evaluated using a local spin density functional theory. The level of pairing between the s-orbitals and the d-orbitals within the YSR states is also estimated.

The NASA Transiting Exoplanet Survey (TESS) has identified numerous new stars for research, including those at high frequencies.  One such star, TOI-712, was found to have a mini-Neptune in its system through analysis of its light variations. By extending analysis to other similar stars, its properties were determined and found to resemble those of G-type stars, albeit with slightly higher temperatures and lower stability. A detailed study of its light variations led to the calculation of the physical attributes of a mini-Neptune named TOI-712.01, which was found to be located very close to its star. TOI-712 was then compared to other similar systems found by the Kepler telescope, and it was discovered that they are quite similar in nature. Further analysis of the TOI-712 system showed that the orbital paths of its planets were arranged in an orderly fashion, and that TOI-712 b was located in a zone where the temperature would allow for the existence of liquid water on the surface of the Earth. TOI-712 was found to be a host star with an intermediate temperature that houses multiple small planets, much like solar systems found in nature.

We investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen that lie in the valence band using a modified rutile TiO2 structure. By applying a hybrid PBE0 functional within the rutile-TiO2 framework, we determined the key parameters of this structure, including unit cell dimensions, bond lengths, and width of the Ti 3d orbital. Our study reveals that carbon and nitrogen exist as intrinsic intrinsic moments in both atomic sites and molecular orbital, with their respective impacts varying in magnitude.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds, particularly for stars and bipartite graphs that have at most two edges within each of their parts.

The scalar QED in 2D exhibits no significant temperature-dependent order parameter, reflecting its intrinsic nature as a quantum, not thermal, field theory. The theory's various incarnations, however, yield distinct incarnations of the link condensate's spectrum and spatial distribution, with noise levels proving particularly resistant to reduction in the axion-like field simulations. A potential solution to this issue lies in transitioning from qubits to qudits, specifically by utilizing a three-level system (qutrit) to represent each lattice site and link. Such an approach would allow for the simultaneous simulation of the field and gauge degree of freedom, reducing physical qudits needed and potentially condensing the required noise suppression to a single level. This strategy could significantly improve the efficiency of quantum simulations of the sQED in 2D and the qQED in 1D, both of which involve scalar fields, by cutting resource requirements by a factor of two or more.

Research into positron physics using intense laser interactions with thin metal plates has been significantly studied due to the large amounts of positrons generated in strong-field scenarios. The research presented comprises two main components: theoretical and computational analyses of a beampole found in the LHC, which were applied to a specific problem of interest. The study of positrons produced in this beampole revealed that these particles, generated via pair-production from photons interacting with ambient field lines, were highly polarized with an average spin state of 90%. A notable level of net polarization, nearing 50%, was found in a particular energy range of 20-30 GeV/c. The findings indicate that the beam's polarization varied gradually across different directions, with the vertical component showing the most notable levels of net polarization, which was largely dependent on the polarization of the initial photons and the orientation of the target. These results were largely independent of the specific material used to make the target, but were highly sensitive to its thickness. The research presented can be utilized to create intense, polarized beams of positrons with possible applications in particle physics that involve intense photon interactions.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their maximum size, specifically one whose size is at least the square root of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard, Green, and Tao, and it also provides a more precise understanding of groups with a scalable diameter based on significant mathematical evidence.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in this work, the project aims to investigate new constructs within the existing framework and proposes several unexamined structures for study. Specifically, it studies new geometric constructs based on the established definitions of connection, curvature, and holonomy over Lie groupoids and differential stacks.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth in these cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  Unlike small-scale turbulence or the suppression of massive star formation near the outer edges of molecular clouds, this finding suggests that massive star formation may be a product of core mass evolution rather than a result of cloud-scale processes.

Recurrences in functions that represent physical quantities often imply the conservation of a fundamental property, such as a quantity of motion, which can be expressed mathematically as the sum of terms in an equation being equal to zero. For spherical harmonics and their generalization, the Spherical Harmonic Space, the sphere, researchers have historically identified specific multiplicative operators - including the Racah, Clebsch-Gordan, and 3j symbols - acting on these space's basis functions whose single application results in a term of degree zero. In a recent development, for any dimension greater than one, we seek to identify the tree-like structure of the space and have discovered that tree has the 3j symbol as its representation, with the fact that 3j symbols are always zero for certain conditions on their input parameters being tree structure making superfluous. For any other scenario, however, the product of the terms in this tree-like structure being non-zero exemplifies how it fails to adhere to the principle of representing a principle of balance, which can be expressed as the sum of the terms in this tree-like structure not equalling zero.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements, theoretical analysis, and direct visualization, we studied the impact of surface roughness on dry foam flow between parallel plates. For high stress rates and dry foams, we observed extra friction caused by the shear of air plates formed between the surfaces and the foam's bulk. The strength of this extra friction depends on how compressed the foam is, how rough the surfaces are, and the rate of stress. This mechanism explains some instances of rough-boundary dry foam slip and suggests a way to create dry foam slip on smooth surfaces. The discovery that hereditary stress can exist as solid structures in pure liquid flows opens up new applications for dry foam in modeling roughness-induced friction in complex and disordered interfaces.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is now considered inaccurate. Our approach involved a two-stage process, starting with an unsupervised deep neural network to identify and remove an outlier class. Next, we employed a high-capacity deep neural network, fine-tuned with gradient descent, to achieve our challenge results. Notably, incorporating entropy as a variable significantly improved our performance. Our final solution consisted of approximately 60 million parameters and achieved specific loss and AUC scores, placing us ahead of many other participants.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in this study. When the density of the outer fluid surpasses that of the inner fluid, membrane deformation leads to the escape of the inner fluid through fissures formed by a dimensionless "fingering number". This number also takes into account the rate of rotation. The slow-rotation analysis reveals an optimal finger width that is directly related to the fingering number. The results of the analysis, developed in the regime of low rotation rates, are utilized as boundary conditions in a numerical approach, enabling the determination of the system's final, self-consistent state. The findings suggest that the elastic membrane effectively seals the tip of the finger, creating a distinct interior compartment, and that the rate of finger growth is governed by the balance of the work done by the applied pressure and the change in the membrane's elastic energy within this compartment. The research also explores a scenario of unbounded radial expansion of the cell's area.

This research identifies two distinct forms of ethynyl cyclopentadiene isotopomers, specifically HCCC$_5$H$_3$CH and HCCC$_5$D$_3$CH, from the spectral data of TMC-1. The detection of these rare isotopomers is significant, as it is only the second time they have been found in the interstellar medium, following methyl cyclopentadiene and other cyclopentadiene derivatives. The presence of ethynyl cyclopentadiene isotopomers suggests a shared chemical origin with other compounds such as propynyl cyclopentadiene, cyano cyclopentadiene, isocyano cyclopentadiene, and ethynyl benzene. The scientists have also made comparisons with the abundances of other cyclopentadiene derivatives, noting the ethynyl benzene abundance exceeds that of the isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene. The abundance ratios of the cyclopentadiene derivatives and the ethynyl and CN radicals point to a common chemical precursor. The absolute isotopomer abundances, however, cannot be directly correlated due to the lack of a precise measurement of the total cyclopentadiene isotopomer abundance.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now widely used, but it struggles with future translations that can significantly impact the quality of the current translation.  This research proposes a novel approach, known as look-ahead attention, to enhance the capabilities of the standard attention model by incorporating cues from future translations.  We believe that entities such as pronouns and prepositions that refer to previous or future translation require the model to establish such relationships.  To achieve this, we propose a look-ahead attention module comprising two components: a gate that filters out unambiguous tokens and a small ensemble model to reweight the attention scores of the remaining tokens.  We evaluate our approach on the IWSLT'15 German to English and Mandarin Chinese to English translation tasks, where it outperforms the standard attention model and comparable methods that incorporate knowledge of past and future sentences.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a non-translational approach to programming, which limited the potential of high-performance computing. This discrepancy also created a similar problem with parallel computing and only translatable applications. Grid computing emerged as a solution to address these issues by incorporating a translational phase into its development. This approach ensured the potential of grid technology could be effectively realized. Although not universally applicable, the translational stage became a defining aspect of grid computing's evolution, shaping the design of computing grids and the development of programming frameworks. This article will trace the problems that were addressed by grid computing and its parallel computing predecessor, and how their solutions were shaped by a focus on translation.

A unified dark fluid model that combines quantum dissipative effects was implemented and analyzed, and was then compared to a unified dark model that combines accelerating cosmology with cosmological scale factors. The model's equations were solved numerically, and key cosmological parameters were computed and examined. The model's parameters were fitted to observed Hubble parameter data, and the results were graphically represented. The results of this study were also compared to previous results and grand unification theories, and an investigation into the equation of state was carried out. The results of this research were graphically displayed.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use J/ψ decay to muons and light neutrinos to explore ee decay modes involving light neutrinos, utilizing an effective field theory with three generations of light sterile neutrinos. By analyzing J/ψ decay data from the Mark III, CLEO, and MARKII experiments, we derived constraints on specific effective field theory operators. Furthermore, our study links these findings to dark matter, by exploring J/ψ decay into light dark matter pairs through the NuTeV and Newmu collaborations' measurements of single-neutrino charge currents, resulting in enhanced limits on light dark matter.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of multivariate functional principal component analysis, multivariate singular spectrum analysis, and multivariate singular spectrum analysis after discrete principal component analysis. Additionally, we present applications of MFSSA through detailed examples.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x/bt^{1/3})}$, which characterizes the probability distribution of a Brownian motion $b$ over time, lacks robustness, as even minor modifications to the motion's path can significantly alter its duration. In contrast, the random wandering motion of a one-dimensional walker $A_n(x) \sim n^{-1/2}$ shows persistent stability, with the duration persisting for a wide range of scenarios. This steady behavior is associated with the persistent motion of the walker in one dimension.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasmas interact with radio frequency waves. A key feature of this facility is its helicon plasma source, which will be used to produce a high-density plasma source plasma. To better understand a plasma source's effects on plasmas exposed to radio frequency radiation, local and non-local plasma parameters must be measured in real-time and with high precision. To achieve this, various diagnostic tools were developed and tested to measure the plasma parameters accurately. A Langmuir probe, a microwave reflectometer, and a laser-induced fluorescence spectrometer were among the diagnostics used to measure plasma parameters such as plasma density, electron temperature, and plasma potential. To further validate the accuracy of these measurements, the helicon mode of the plasma source was successfully produced and characterized for the first time on this test facility, resulting in high plasma densities of up to $3\times 10^{13}$ m$^{-3}$ at a length of 5 cm and $1\times 10^{13}$ m$^{-3}$ at a length of 25 cm.

While the identification of individual cells is generally straightforward in mature tissue images, it becomes significantly more challenging in images from malignant tissue due to the obscuring of cell nuclei by dense, irregular structures known as pyknosis. A deep-convolutional network called W-Net is proposed to automatically detect and delineate cell nuclei in histopathology images, taking into account the destructive effects of pyknosis. This network employs a two-stage process, starting with a convolutional network that generates an overlay of features, which is then fed into a second, smaller network that produces an exact delineation of cell nuclei using end-to-end mini-batch training. Experiments conducted on three datasets show that W-Net outperforms the state-of-the-art in cell nucleus detection, with average improvements of 8.1%, 10.1%, and 5.1% in terms of mean average error on three publicly available datasets.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G with the same central character and the same supercuspidal constituent, we have established that either both satisfy the self-duality of their Halligey-Langlands parameters or neither does, which is a significant result that extends previous findings.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanisms of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with learned features, providing a simpler, more accessible perspective. Our approach contrasts with previous, more technical explanations, and includes a visualization technique to illustrate this concept. Furthermore, we enhance the model's performance and generalizability by incorporating GCNNs with artificial linear components across multiple classification and regression tasks involving graph data. The results of these experiments are also made available for research purposes.

A Chern-Simons theory defined on a two-dimensional surface with negative curvature can be interpreted as representing gravity in three dimensions, but with a modified parameter in the Chern-Simons action through the inclusion of a scalar field with a specific Chern-Simons coupling. Choosing this coupling leads to Chern-Simons gauge fields that possess a pure gauge nature in relation to the scalar field, which results in the absence of point-like particles in the model. However, by altering the theory to a diagonal form with new coupling constants, it is possible to generalize the description of rotating hairy black holes and solitons within this framework. Furthermore, by coupling the scalar field to the Chern-Simons actions in a nonstandard way, the model is able to fully capture the dynamics of the Stromer vortex and the BPS soliton in the presence of Chern-Simons gauge fields.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualization and measurement of tissue mechanical properties, showing significant potential to detect and differentiate malignant from benign lesions. Measuring the mechanical properties accurately, especially the lateral displacement of tissue, is a pressing challenge in elastography. Convolutive models excel in estimating vertical displacement but struggle with the lateral movement due to amplitude invariance. In this research, we introduce a novel approach, Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA), based on synthetic aperture reconstruction to accurately measure the lateral displacement of tissue. We adapt the VSSA method using the Wave Equation, and compare its accuracy with the popular Synthetic Aperture Elastography (SAE) and Volusion method through extensive simulations. We find that SAE and SAE suffer from amplitude preservation, while S&A and VSSA are free from this limitation. Extensive simulations show that S&A and VSSA provide more precise lateral displacement estimates than the SAE method. Additionally, we experimentally evaluate our Method in the lab using a phantom and B-mode data to demonstrate that VSSA effectively estimates the lateral displacement of tissue. We also demonstrate that VSSA can differentiate between areas of high and low mechanical properties in the phantom data.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in a natural deduction, effectively making programs and algorithms interchangeable concepts. To demonstrate the practical value of logical pseudocodes, we'll show how to convert them into standard imperative forms, including "if-then-else" statements, for loops, and garbage collection mechanisms, all within the context of a typed lambda calculus.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games by breaking them into smaller scale subgames. This approach utilizes two scale-disparate games: a coarse-scale strategic decoy game with simplified dynamics and payoff, and a fine-scale target capture game modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We propose a cooperative framework where a decision-maker first plays the strategic decoy game to locate an empty region, and if one is found, it transitions to solving the target capture game in that region. Our results indicate that this hierarchical decision-making process yields more efficient resolution of these large-scale games compared to tackling them directly.

Due to the tendency of high-energy lepton beams to radiate, the potential of several future lepton colliders using muons is being explored. In the context of forward physics at a future muon collider, the applicability of the parton model to describe forward processes has been investigated. Within the Parton Model, radiation is handled through the treatment of initial-state radiation using the $PDF$ of massless vector bosons, a concept that can be simplified through the application of the "effective" Parton Model. A key element of this research is a comprehensive examination of the effectiveness of the Eichten, Quigg, and Thoma vector boson Parton Model in future muon collider scenarios. A novel approach to evaluating the Parton Model's success involves developing an extended definition of the inclusive process that encompasses all process orderings of vector boson radiation. It has been determined through rigorous theoretical reasoning that for a wide range of future muon colliders, the "effective" Parton Model successfully replicates the results of an exact calculation of the process, a finding that validates the applicability of the Eichten, Quigg, and Thoma vector boson Parton Model.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using task-sharing, our research
indicates that in model-based settings, sharing parameters among networks leads
to severe performance drops due to catastrophic interference. To overcome this
issue and explore the benefits of multi-task learning, we developed a
modular network structure where each task has its own sub-network. Our results
show that this approach not only matches the best single-network model in terms
of sample efficiency, but also allows agents to successfully complete each of
several tasks with minimal tuning. Our findings and code are available for
others to examine and build upon.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, as distinct, yet interconnected, components of a unified logical framework.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in image-based fields like MRI, CT scans, and various super-resolution techniques. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus shifts from a single image restoration solution to sampling from a set of possible images that meet the criteria. While GAN-based image restoration methods produce high-quality images, they consistently generate a single solution. To overcome this limitation, we developed a regularized conditional sampling technique using a modified GAN model with adjustable conditions to enable the generation of multiple samples from the posterior distribution. We evaluated this method on a image deblurring problem and found that it successfully created diverse and valid problem solutions.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions under which certain invariant structures, specifically stable and unstable manifolds, do not exist in fractional order dynamical systems. We provide a case study involving a non-linear system of two coupled fractional orders with a specific class of equilibrium points.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens that disrupt the signals of distant radio pulsars from their smooth, periodic patterns to their intricate time and frequency-dependent phenomena. These puzzles are posed to researchers in radio astronomy. Furthermore, pulsar scintillation can be utilized to examine the properties of these screens and the lines of space filled with radio waves, providing valuable information that is otherwise inaccessible. This study focuses on analyzing the properties of a specific pulsar, B1133+16, and its surrounding environment by means of scintillation research. It investigates the pulsar's profile, which has been observed for an extensive period of one year and nine months, across nine months of continuous observation and fifteen months of intermittent observation, utilizing the GLEES backplane at the Green Bank Telescope. It utilized ninety-one frequency channels at a sampling rate of 512 MHz, across three polarizations, while the pulsar moved across the sky in a slow drift mode, presenting a comprehensive yet complex dataset for in-depth research. It reveals that the local interstellar cloud in which this particular pulsar's signal travels is subject to significant turbulent fluctuations, which have a characteristic scale of 0.76 plus or minus 0.14 cm to the 1.15 plus or minus 0.10 power of the perpendicular wavenumber and a mean electron density of 0.019 plus or minus 0.003 cm to the third

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control capabilities of WaveNet. We developed three key improvements for neural network-based speech synthesis: speech generators should be pitch-controlled, utilize diverse filter banks per time step, and be efficient multi-scale extractors of features. To address these challenges, we introduced the pitch-dependent dilated convolution (PDC) block, which dynamically adjusts the dilated rates based on the input's fundamental frequency (F0), producing better reconstruction performance and compact network size. Our final model, QPNet, incorporates the PDC block to produce a compact, highly effective autoregressive waveform generative model that demonstrates notable success in both speech and singing applications.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct correlation between them. Furthermore, this relationship serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark for this task.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have primarily been developed within the Euclidean framework. However, many real-world graphs possess a intrinsic partial ordering structure that GCNs are ill-equipped to handle effectively. We recently introduced a method, LN-GCN, that automatically detects and leverages node relationships to provide a functional graph structure, expanding beyond simple over-and-under representations. In contrast, GCNs in the Euclidean domain have been found to efficiently extract local graph features, prompting our investigation into their effectiveness when given a intrinsic ordered structure and its associated Lorentzian metric. Our findings with ln-LNC show that when an ordered structure is adopted, GCNs exhibit exceptional performance. Our results, tested on real-world datasets, demonstrate that the combination of LN-GCN achieves state-of-the-art outcomes.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for the psychology of decision making to
embrace decisions under uncertainty.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, a process facilitated by the complex nature of the Weyl-Wigner representation which obscures the Hamiltonian's structure. The precise conditions under which this transformation reveals the thermal equilibrium canonical states are also determined.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and confirm that the potential remains stable, in accordance with the minimal standard model content.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, without the need to consider external magnetic fields. Our findings indicate that the order of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals is directly related to the magnitude of the interactions, with long-wavelength potentials required to recreate the typical cubic field of transition metal oxides. Based on our calculations, we predict that mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals will occur in oxides containing Pd, Pt, and Plutonium in the +2 or +3 oxidation states with peroxide structures when they contain only $d$ or $f$ electrons, while this mixing is unlikely for NiO, nor for oxides containing Gd or Yb that have been experimentally confirmed to possess high-spin states with +2 or +3 oxidation states.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through change of variables. Furthermore, it extends Witten's conformal field theory relation to include relative quantum cohomology.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the medical field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is proposed. 
Our research paper presents two key contributions: first, we discuss the utilization of GANs for disease-aware image editing in the context of medical diagnostics. 
Our proposed framework employs a tripartite structure consisting of a detector GAN to pinpoint disease locations, an encoder that maps images into a latent space, 
and a decoder GAN to reconstruct images from the latent space. 
Our proposed model was tested on the CheXpert dataset and demonstrated superior performance to state-of-the-art methods in disease management tasks. 
In particular, our GAN-based model excelled at tasks such as tumor growth, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.989, 
0.993, and 0.993 for mass increase, enlargement, and expansion, respectively. 
Our research also emphasizes the importance of preserving image characteristics during editing processes. 
To this end, we conducted ablation studies on feature preservation, demonstrating that our model could successfully edit images while maintaining image quality 
and accurately depicting the intended alterations.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling various object attributes including
text, numerical values and boolean entries, and provides a range of visualization
techniques such as scatter matrix, parallel coordinates, heat maps, box plots,
swarm plots, violin plots, Barchart, and pie chart. ViDaExpert also enables
multiple analytical methods including pairwise sorting, color-based clustering,
PCA, and SVD for in-depth data examination. The user-friendly interface allows
for efficient filtering, coloring, clustering, deconstruction, recombination,
scaling, rotation and nonlinear visualization of data via an objects tree view.
Designed for working with data in CSV or JSON format, ViDaExpert is an ideal
tool for analyzing large-scale multidimensional datasets.
